name: Aaron Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. You can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. To begin, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Kestrel Farm for a farming partnership of three families: 220 dairy cows, 300 acres of grass and maize, and about 250 acres of wheat. We already have four robot milkers, so my morning starts on my phone, checking which cows didn't visit the robot overnight and why. Then it's the drone pictures of the wheat, a chat with an AI tool about the feed ration, and the rest of the day I'm in boots with the team of five. I like that mix a lot.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The alarms at two in the morning when a robot milker jams. And the partners, honestly: three families means three opinions on every tractor we buy. At home it's just me and my partner Tom, who tests software for an insurance firm from our spare room. We rent, we've got about four months of savings, and we're arguing gently about whether to try for a mortgage next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly, because I'd hoped for better tools. On the farmers' forum I'd post that the robot milkers were the real revolution and AI was the icing. I'd still argue the gains from the tools we've got should go to workers, not just the partners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means things stay good for us. My job's secure, Tom's job's secure, and Kestrel is doing alright on milk prices. The only real pressure is rent and the mortgage question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running Kestrel and keep using the AI ration tool, because it saves us about 3 percent on feed. We'd go ahead with the mortgage, probably for a small terrace in the village next spring. I'd try a newer drone mapping app on the maize too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little let down. Fine is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the gains should go to workers. What does that mean at Kestrel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the robot milkers came in, nobody lost a job, but the partners kept all the savings. I'd push for a bonus scheme so the team gets a share of whatever the feed savings come to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you less calm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A milk price crash, honestly. That's always the real worry for dairy, AI or no AI. We'd still be fine for a year on our savings, but the partners might stop investing.

say: The **robot milkers** were the real revolution and AI was the icing.
Any gains from tools should **reach workers**, not only owners.
think: My job and **Tom's job** both stay secure.
Our only real pressure is **rent** and the **mortgage** decision.
do: **Keep using** the AI ration tool that saves about **3 percent** on feed.
**Buy** a small terrace in the village next spring.
**Push** the partners for a staff **bonus scheme**.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **let down** that the tools didn't get better.
S0.quote: When the robot milkers came in, nobody lost a job, but the partners kept all the savings.
fieldNote: He already works **alongside robots** and AI, so this world feels normal.
His **progressive** streak shows in the push for staff to share gains.
His remaining worry is the **milk price**, not technology.

steps.text: Keep using the AI feed ration tool on the 220 cows
Try a newer drone mapping app on the maize
Take out a mortgage on a village terrace next spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for farms that are ready, and we should help the ones that aren't. I'd post on the forum about what we've learned with the robot milkers. And I'd say loudly that people losing office jobs need real support, not a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job probably gets better. But Tom's job is checking and coding, which is exactly what this card says goes first. If his firm cuts testers, we'd lose more than half our household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the mortgage on hold for a year, straight away. I'd sit down with Tom and help him find a move into something more hands-on or people-facing, maybe a course in the first six months. On the farm I'd bring in the AI planning tools early, and offer to train other managers in the area for a fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited for the farm and knotted up for Tom. Both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Tom say when you first talked about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Tom laughed and said he'd come and drive the tractor. Then Tom went quiet for the whole evening. I think he's more worried than he lets on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if Tom's income drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage plan, then the car payments on Tom's car. We'd get through six months on my wage and our savings, but not much more.

say: This is good for **farms that are ready**, and others need help.
People losing office jobs need **real support**, not a leaflet.
think: My own job probably **gets better** with these tools.
Tom's **software testing** job is exactly the kind that goes first.
do: **Put** the **mortgage** on hold for a year.
**Help** Tom find a course within **six months**.
**Offer** paid training on farm AI tools to other managers.
feel: **Excited** for the farm and **knotted up** for Tom.
S1.quote: My partner Tom laughed and said he'd come and drive the tractor. Then Tom went quiet for the whole evening.
fieldNote: His own job looks safe, but the **household income** is exposed through Tom.
He turns his **AI skills** into a possible side income.
He sounds upbeat in public but is **anxious** in private.

steps.text: Put the village mortgage on hold for a year
Bring AI planning tools into Kestrel's crop and herd work
Charge other farm managers for training on AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is much faster. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income or something like it, and fast, because two years is too short for people to retrain. I'd say it to the partners, on the forum, and to my MP. I'd also say farms will still need people who understand animals and machines together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2028 Tom's job is gone and so is the planning half of mine, the rations and the crop plans. Then by 2031 the robots can do the hands-on half too. I'd have about three years as the person who runs the robots, and then I don't know what I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the mortgage plan and move our savings into an easy-access account. I'd ask the partners for a written role as automation lead, starting now, so I'm the one setting up the robots. I'd get Tom into a course for robot maintenance or animal care by the end of the first year, and I'd write to our MP about income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake running the numbers, because both our jobs are on the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the one setting up the robots. Isn't that speeding up your own exit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I've thought about it. Somebody will set up those robots, and I'd rather it's me, so I'm the last one out and I know how it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jess, our herd assistant. She's 22 and brilliant with calves, and she's exactly the person who'd lose out in 2031. I'd want to get her trained on the robot side too.

say: We need a **basic income** or similar, because two years is too short.
Farms will still need people who understand **animals and machines**.
think: Tom's job and my **planning work** both go by **2028**.
By **2031** robots take the hands-on half of my job too.
do: **Cancel** the mortgage plan and keep savings **easy to reach**.
**Ask** the partners for a written **automation lead** role.
**Get** Tom into a robot maintenance course within a year.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless, because **both jobs** are on the clock.
S2.quote: Somebody will set up those robots, and I'd rather it's me, so I'm the last one out and I know how it works.
fieldNote: He expects **both household incomes** to go, which is why he's alarmed.
He knowingly **speeds up** his own exit to stay in control.
He thinks about **junior staff** like Jess, not only himself.

steps.text: Cancel the mortgage plan and keep savings in easy access
Take on the automation lead role at Kestrel Farm
Enrol Tom in a robot maintenance course this year
Write to the MP asking for income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the slower version. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if governments start now. I'd post on the forum about how farms can move staff into new roles instead of sacking them. And I'd say we should start talking about who owns the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is much easier to handle. Tom has three or four years to move, and by 2031 the AI does the planning side of my job. I'd still have until about 2034 on the hands-on and robot side, and by then I'd want to be doing something else anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd help Tom choose a new direction, and he'd start part-time study. I'd ask the partners for the automation lead role and get them to pay for a course in farm robotics. We'd delay the mortgage two years and save about 300 a month instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. I'd have a list and a timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe advising farms on robots and animal welfare, or running a co-op that shares robots between small farms. Something where I'm still outdoors at least half the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep mentioning ownership. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because whoever owns the robots gets the money. If small farms and their workers own them through a co-op, the gains stay in the village instead of going to some company miles away.

say: Five years is **enough** if governments **start now**.
Farms can move staff into **new roles** instead of sacking them.
We should talk about **who owns** the robots.
think: Tom has **three or four years** to change direction.
I'd want to be in a **new role** before robots arrive in **2034**.
do: **Help** Tom start part-time study in the first year.
**Ask** the partners to pay for a **farm robotics** course.
**Delay** the mortgage two years and save **300 a month**.
feel: **Anxious** in a useful way, with a list and a timeline.
S3.quote: Whoever owns the robots gets the money.
fieldNote: The extra years turn his alarm into a **planned transition** for both of them.
He keeps returning to **ownership**, a sign of his politics.
He still expects real **income risk**, so anxious rather than uneasy.

steps.text: Take a partner-funded course in farm robotics
Save about 300 a month instead of paying a deposit
Delay buying a house for two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty if we plan, and I'd want our local farmers' group to start a robot-sharing co-op now. I'd post about it, too. And I'd still push for public support, because not everyone has my head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one's fine for me. I'd be 37 when AGI arrives and 40 when the robots do. By then I'd hope to be running a co-op, and Tom would have years to move. A robot-sharing co-op with four or five neighbouring farms is the job I'd actually want in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go ahead with the mortgage next spring, as planned. Over the next two or three years I'd set up a robot-sharing co-op with four or five neighbouring farms, putting in maybe 5,000 of our own savings. Tom would start a part-time course in the next year or two, without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit of a buzz, actually, because I can see a job I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting 5,000 into a co-op is a big part of four months' savings. Why risk it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd have years to earn it back and I'd be building something I believe in. If it fails, I've still got my job at Kestrel for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this one that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's job, a little. Even ten years goes quickly when you're busy, and I'd hate him to leave it too late.

say: A **decade** is plenty if we plan.
Local farms should start a **robot-sharing co-op** now.
Not everyone has my head start, so **public support** still matters.
think: I'd be **40** when robots arrive, with time to build something new.
**Tom** has years to move without panic.
do: **Buy** the village terrace next spring as planned.
**Put** about **5,000** into a robot-sharing co-op with neighbours.
**Encourage** Tom to start a part-time course within two years.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with a **buzz** about a job I'd like.
S4.quote: A robot-sharing co-op with four or five neighbouring farms is the job I'd actually want in ten years.
fieldNote: With ten years he sees **opportunity** rather than threat.
He is willing to **risk savings** on a co-op he believes in.
His one worry is **Tom** leaving it too late.

steps.text: Buy a small terrace in the village next spring
Put about 5,000 into a robot-sharing co-op with neighbours
Support Tom into a part-time course within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Tom and I would both be out of work within three years of each other. What would help is a proper income floor while people retrain, and public money for farm co-ops that own their own robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Robots are great at routine, but a sick cow at two in the morning still needs someone who knows the herd. I'd want that kept in whatever rules get written.

headlineQuote: A sick cow at two in the morning still needs someone who knows the herd.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** manager of a 600-acre dairy and arable farm with four robot milkers.
He uses **AI tools daily** and is comfortable taking risks on new technology.
His partner Tom is a **software tester**, so the household's risk sits mostly with Tom.
He is calm in AI Plateau, **alarmed** in AGI by 2028 and calm again with ten years.
He believes **who owns the robots** decides who benefits, and dreams of a farm co-op.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he and Tom would both lose work within three years.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for farm **co-ops** that own their robots.
